Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-06-02

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick roll call — can we confirm we have Marissa, Ibrahim, Leah, and Ravi?
[00:12] Marissa: Yep that's right, Marissa here.
[00:14] Ibrahim: Ibrahim, on the infra side.
[00:17] Leah: Leah, compliance.
[00:19] Ravi: Ravi, network.
[00:22] Samir: Awesome. Jules and Tess from our side will cover the technical bits — primarily the private deployment topology and how we wire in KMS and egress controls.
[00:32] Jules: Hi all. Quick agenda: SOC2/ISO evidence, RBAC/SSO & SCIM, audit logs and SIEM hooks, KMS options (Redwood-managed vs customer-managed/HSM), and the airlock/egress proxy pattern we've used with other regulated customers.
[00:48] Marissa: Great. First thing, where can we see your SOC2 and ISO certs? We need the full attestations for our audit team, and the control matrix.
[00:56] Samir: I'll send the PDFs after the call — SOC2 Type II report, ISO27001 certificate, and a compliance matrix mapping our controls to common frameworks. LINK: https://redwood.example.com/compliance (note: raw links often truncated in transcription)
[01:12] Leah: When you say "private deployment", is that the same as the VPC option where the control plane is in your cloud but data plane stays in our VPC? We need firm guarantees around no egress outside the region.
[01:26] Jules: Good question. We offer a Private mode where a thin control plane is hosted but models run in your VPC. For strict residency we also support a fully private control plane and on-prem package. For Avalon we recommended the VPC private option with control plane peered or via private link, and explicit routing that pins compute to us-east-2 — is that the region you're planning?
[01:47] Ibrahim: Yes, us-east-2 for production. We have requirements that logs and snapshots never leave that region.
[01:52] Jules: We can enforce regional affinity in the orchestration layer and in the routing policy. We also support an airlock egress proxy pattern — requests from the model nodes to the outside world go through an egress box you control, with allowlists and deep inspection.
[02:10] Ravi: Can you clarify the egress box design? We're thinking of a hardened proxy in a separate subnet with a static IP and strict outbound rules, plus TLS inspection. How do you handle updates to allowlists for model downloads or OS patches?
[02:25] Tess: Typically customers run a bastion/proxy that we call an "egress gateway". The pattern: model nodes are in private subnets with no internet. For outbound they NAT through the egress gateway. We sign and verify binaries and also support a pull-only update model to limit inbound. For allowlists, we recommend a small set of destination FQDNs/IPs; we can provide the list for model pulls and licensing endpoints — but you must host or permit access from those addresses.
[02:50] Marissa: We require HSM-backed keys for any customer-managed KMS. Can your runtime use an external KMS with key encryption where we hold the KEK?
[02:59] Jules: Yes, we support envelope encryption. The model runtime only sees wrapped keys; unwrapping happens in your KMS/HSM. We integrate with common clouds' KMS (KMS, CloudKMS), and support external HSMs over PKCS#11 — there might be minor configuration work for on-prem HSMs.
[03:18] Leah: How does audit logging work? Our auditors want immutable logs with at least 7 years retention, SAML login events, admin role changes, model version rollouts, and per-token usage records for high-risk endpoints.
[03:33] Samir: We stream audit events via an event connector to your SIEM (S3, Kafka, or direct CloudWatch/Stackdriver). Logs include admin activity, SSO/SSO failures, model deploy events, and token-level metadata. For very long retention we recommend archival to an S3 bucket under your account with object lock and lifecycle rules.
[03:54] Marissa: Object lock is mandatory for us.
[03:56] Jules: That's fine — we can push to your bucket and you can enable governance/retention. We also provide a tamper-evident checksum and signed log bundles if you want independent verification.
[04:12] Ibrahim: Network ACLs and microsegmentation — do you support host hardening and PAM? Like, can we restrict which hosts can access the KV cache and metrics?
[04:22] Tess: Yes. We run services on distinct subnets and groups; internal service mesh or iptables rules can tightly limit intra-VPC traffic. For KV cache we use mutual TLS between nodes and token-based auth; we can add additional mTLS at the application layer if needed.
[04:36] Ravi: One concern — latency when encryption is on and KMS calls go to the HSM in our DC. Has anyone measured the p99 impact of external KMS unwrapping?
[04:47] Jules: On unwrap operations at startup the hit is minimal (tens of milliseconds), because we cache ephemeral DEKs (data encryption keys) in memory or in secure KV; unwrap is used infrequently. For per-request signing you get more impact. We can run a perf trial with your HSM; Jules: will pick a small sample and run 100 qps with encryption-on.
[05:06] Marissa: Good. Also, regarding RBAC — we need fine-grained role separation: platform admins vs model ops vs security read-only. Do you support custom roles and SCIM provisioning from our IdP?
[05:18] Samir: Yes, SCIM provisioning is supported and roles are customizable. SSO via SAML/OIDC and SCIM for group sync. Also audit trail for role changes.
[05:28] Leah: Do you support separation of duties for key admins vs platform admins? We want a different admin who can rotate keys but not deploy models.
[05:37] Tess: We support KMS role separation because key operations are proxied to your KMS and governed by your IAM policies. On the Redwood side you can control who can request operations; combined with your KMS policies we can implement separation.
[05:52] Ravi: Let's talk egress filtering more concretely — whitelists vs allowlists, and how to handle model telemetry. Some of the earlier comps leaked telemetry to third-party endpoints.
[06:05] Jules: We can disable telemetry and outbound pings by default in private installs. For hosted telemetry we can route into your telemetry collector only. The airlock enforces mediations and deep packet inspection if you have an NGFW; otherwise we recommend a small managed proxy that only resolves signed endpoints.
[06:21] Ibrahim: For the control plane connectivity, do we need a persistent VPN or only control-plane API calls over PrivateLink?
[06:29] Samir: Both are options. PrivateLink is typically sufficient for API calls and control messages. For extra isolation some customers prefer an IPsec VPN for administrative sessions or a full private control plane.
[06:41] Marissa: On certs and mTLS — how are the certificates provisioned and rotated? We need automated, auditable rotation for at least leaf certs every 90 days.
[06:51] Tess: We support automated certificate issuance — you can bring your CA or use our internal CA with rotation hooks. For strict compliance, bring-your-own-CA integrated with your PKI is the recommended path; Redwood's runtime will call renewal hooks and we log rotation events.
[07:05] Ravi: Which ports and protocols need to be opened between the control plane and nodes? We need a minimal list for our firewall team.
[07:11] Jules: Minimal ports: outbound 443 for control-plane API (TCP 443), mTLS endpoints on configurable high ports for internal mesh (we can provide the exact port ranges), and ephemeral for agent heartbeats. We'll document precisely in the diagram.
[07:25] Marissa: Can you walk through an example end-to-end flow for a request that touches PII and needs to stay in-region?
[07:32] Jules: Sure. Example: client app in us-east-2 calls your API which hits a proxy that forwards to model endpoints in the same region. Model nodes have access only to the local S3 bucket for artifacts, and to the egress gateway for controlled outbound. Keys are wrapped in your KMS in us-east-2; unwraps happen in HSM in-region. Audit logs stream to your SIEM in region, and cross-region routing is disabled.
[07:58] Leah: That sounds good. We need diagrams and an explicit SLA paragraph that says data won't egress outside us-east-2 except via an approved exception process.
[08:07] Samir: We can include contractual language in the DPA and SLA. I'll work with legal to add a data residency clause.
[08:14] Ravi: On the firewall rules: will you provide a suggested iptables/Cisco ASA config? We need to ensure our hardware supports the model.
[08:22] Jules: Yes we'll produce sample ACLs and NAT rules for both cloud-managed and on-prem firewalls. We'll include examples for Palo Alto, Cisco ASA, and iptables so your team has a drop-in template.
[08:34] Marissa: About monitoring and incident response — if there's a suspected exfiltration, what tools do you expose for traceability?
[08:41] Tess: We provide request-level traces, per-token activity logs, and we can export full packet captures via your egress gateway if you choose. We also ship a timeline of model rollouts and config changes. Those artifacts are timestamped and signed.
[08:58] Ibrahim: Can we get an offline verification bundle — something we can hand to auditors without giving access to runtime?
[09:04] Samir: Yes, we can provide signed bundles: audit logs, model hashes, deploy manifests, and a signed attestation that the release ID matches what's in your environment. We'll also give checksums to validate.
[09:18] Leah: For key rotation cadence — what's a practical rota without impacting performance? We prefer 30-90 day rotations for DEKs.
[09:27] Jules: Rotating DEKs every 30 days is fine if you use envelope keys cached for active sessions. We recommend rotating KEKs less frequently — 90 days — and DEKs more often. We'll show a recommended policy.
[09:41] Marissa: Is your logging tamper-proof? You mentioned checksums, but what prevents a privileged actor from editing logs?
[09:48] Tess: We support streaming to your customer-owned S3 with object lock and can also sign events with a timestamping service. Combined with separation of duties (who can access the archive) this provides tamper-evidence.
[09:58] Ravi: A pragmatic question: what's the lift for our infra to get a staging env up with private deploy? Days, weeks?
[10:05] Jules: For staging on an existing VPC with provided subnets and a KMS endpoint, typical timeline is 2-3 days for initial deploy, then a week to harden firewall rules and run the perf tests. On-prem longer due to hardware and airgap prep.
[10:20] Marissa: Will you do a penetration test as part of onboarding?
[10:24] Samir: We can share our pen-test summary. For customer-specific pentests inside your VPC we can coordinate windows and scope — many customers prefer to run a third-party pentest on their environment post-deploy.
[10:36] Leah: Ok — from compliance perspective, please map your controls to our SOC matrix and note any compensating controls we should document.
[10:44] Samir: We'll do that and include a short list of compensating controls for items that are problematic.
[10:49] Ravi: A couple of jittery items — how do you handle kernel CVEs on nodes that are locked down with your runtime? Who applies patches?
[10:57] Tess: Patching is coordinated: for private deploys we can either push signed kernel updates through your egress pipeline or provide a patch bundle that you deploy. We recommend scheduled maintenance windows and staged rollouts.
[11:09] Jules: Also a note on KV cache — we often see folks call it "KV cash" in notes — it's KV cache (key-value). We protect it with in-memory encryption and mTLS; eviction policies are also plumbed.
[11:20] Small crosstalk / laughter
[11:23] Marissa: Thanks for that clarification.
[11:25] Samir: We're getting close to an operational plan. Next steps — I'll send the attestation docs, Jules will produce the diagram, Ravi will share current firewall exports. Anything else?
[11:35] Leah: Please also include a short write-up of our option: Private control plane vs Hosted thin control plane with PrivateLink — specifically pros/cons for audit and legal.
[11:44] Samir: Will do.
[11:46] Marissa: And pricing is secondary but we need a sense of uplift for a fully private control plane and HSM integration.
[11:52] Samir: We'll include estimated uplift ranges in the follow-up note.
[11:56] Jules: I'll also schedule a deep-dive with Ravi next week to walk through the ACLs.
[12:02] Ravi: Sounds good — please include sample commands for the NAT gateway and route table entries.
[12:07] Samir: Perfect. Any final questions?
[12:10] Leah: None here.
[12:11] Marissa: No. Thanks all.
[12:13] Samir: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up on the items.
